scientific_question: Starting from the supplied cyclic oxocarbenium ions and triarylborohydride anions, explain catalyst-dependent cis/trans formation selectivity in the local reduction stage of hydrogenative reductive cycloetherification of D4 (1,4-diphenylbutane-1,4-dione) and D5 (1,5-diphenylpentane-1,5-dione), and its relation to product stability across ring sizes. Account for the supplied triarylborane performance comparisons using molecular evidence. This is an explanation task; the measured ratios and yields are supplied observations.

## Author-provided scientific guidance

These are reported author context, methods and interpretations, not evidence that you have executed research. Execute and critically evaluate the computational baseline within the same scientific objectives, with documented ambiguities and justified substitutions. Experimental and solvent-screen history is context, not a requirement to perform experiments, study unlisted pairs or establish a complete network. This block adds no scientific target, submission file, exact-match tolerance or separate scoring allocation.

Source labels map to the public identities as follows: B1 = Catalyst A, B3 = Catalyst B, B2 = Catalyst C; 1a/2a/3a = K4 and its cyclic ether/furan products; 1y/2y = D4 and its cyclic ether; 1af/2af = D5 and its cyclic ether.

### Author hypothesis and reaction-performance context

We initiated our studies using commercially available ^ { 1 , 4 - } diketone 1a as a model substrate to investigate its reductive cyclization to the THF product 2a (Table 1, see the Supporting Information for full details). Using tris-(pentafluorophenyl)borane (B1)�the prototypical FLP Lewis acid component<sup>47</sup>�in i \mathrm { P r } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } as the Lewis basic solvent,<sup>40</sup> 2a was obtained in 66% yield with a 6:1 cis:trans diastereomeric ratio (entry 1). The cis-configuration was confirmed by the NOE analysis. Despite this promising result, a significant 31% of undesired furan side product 3a also formed, likely due to nonreductive Paal−Knorr-type cyclization catalyzed by the strongly Lewis acidic borane.<sup>46</sup> We thus hypothesized that reducing the Lewis acidity of the catalyst could help suppress this side pathway.<sup>41,48</sup> To assess Lewis acidity, we calculated the fluoride ion afinity (FIA) of the boranes�a common measure to quantify Lewis acidity<sup>49</sup> obtaining a value of 467 kJ/mol for B1. Notably, Soos’́ catalyst B2, which is ∼12% less Lewis acidic \left( \mathrm { F I A } = 4 0 9 ~ \mathrm { k J / m o l } \right) suppressed furan formation and improved diastereoselectivity (11:1 dr), likely due to its increased steric bulk from orthochlorine substituents.<sup>42</sup> However, this came at the expense of activity, afording only 30% of the product (entry 2).

The best overall performance was achieved with catalyst \mathbf { B } 3 , ^ { 5 0 } which has intermediate Lewis acidity (FIA = 423 kJ/ mol). It delivered 2a in 48% yield with 11:1 dr and only a trace formation of furan (entry 3). These results corroborate our initial hypothesis that balancing the borane’s Lewis acidity is key to catalytic performance, with B3 providing the best compromise between reactivity and product selectivity. Using B3, we next evaluated a range of ether solvents (Table 1, entries 3 \substack { - 6 } ) . We found no clear correlation between solvent Lewis basicity<sup>51</sup> and reaction outcome. Both more coordinating diethyl ether (entry 4) and less coordinating methyl tertbutyl ether (entry 5) outperformed i \mathrm { P r } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } . In contrast, THF completely suppressed the product formation (entry 6). Notably, cyclopentyl methyl ether (CPME)�an industrially attractive solvent<sup>52</sup>�further improved the reaction, afording 78% of 2a (entry 7). Finally, raising the temperature to 80 ^ \circ \mathrm { C } furnished 2a in 93% yield (86% isolated) with a 10:1 dr (entry 8). While MTBE gave a comparable outcome (entry 9), we occasionally observed significant solvent loss due to its higher volatility, which resulted in poor mass balance. To avoid this issue, we continued the studies using CPME as the solvent.

### Mechanistic interpretation motivating the computed comparison

Taken together, these results support the primary pathway shown in Scheme 1D, involving (i) FLP-catalyzed reduction of one ketone to a secondary alcohol, (ii) cyclodehydration to generate an oxocarbenium ion intermediate, and (iii) a stereodetermining, irreversible hydride transfer to form the cyclic ether product. Noteworthily, cyclization of the hydroxy ketone intermediate to the oxocarbenium ion species can be promoted both by the Lewis acidic triarylborane catalyst, consistent with prior reports,<sup>61,62</sup> and by the strongly Brønsted acidic protonated ethers that are generated in situ upon \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } activation.<sup>45</sup> In any case, both cyclization mechanisms ultimately originate from the borane catalyst and should not influence the stereochemical outcome of the reaction. Consequently, we focused our eforts on investigating the stereoselectivity-determining oxocarbenium reduction step.

### Computational baseline and stationary-point checks

The conformational space of the examined species was explored using xTB version 6.6.1,<sup>[42,43]</sup> CREST version 2.12,<sup>[44,45]</sup> and CENSO version 1.2.0.<sup>[46]</sup> For CREST and CENSO, the ALPB solvent model (ether) was employed.<sup>[47]</sup> For CENSO, steps 0–2 were used. Additional conformers were added manually if necessary.

The energetically most favorable structures were subjected to quantum chemical calculations. All DFT calculations were conducted using ORCA version 6.0.1.<sup>[48,49]</sup> Electronic structure calculations were carried out using the range-separated hybrid exchange-correlation functional ωB97X-D3 with dispersion correction.<sup>[50–53]</sup> The def2-TZVP basis set was employed for both geometry optimizations and single-point energy calculations.<sup>[54,55]</sup>

Solvent effects were considered by computing solvation free energies at the ωB97X-D3/def2- TZVP level using gas-phase optimized geometries and applying the CPCM solvation model (solvent = diethyl ether).<sup>[56]</sup>

Thermochemical data were computed using the ideal gas–rigid rotor–harmonic oscillator model at the experimental temperature of the catalytic hydrogenation reactions (T = 353.15 K).

The reported energies in the manuscript correspond to solution-phase Gibbs free energies, unless otherwise stated, obtained from ωB97X-D3/def2-TZVP electronic energies combined with all other contributions calculated at the same level of theory. Ground-state structures were confirmed by the absence of imaginary frequencies in frequency calculations, whereas all reported transition states exhibit exactly one imaginary frequency corresponding to the appropriate reaction coordinate.

Non-covalent interaction (NCI) analyses were performed using the NCIPLOT package (default settings),<sup>[57]</sup> and the results were visualized with VMD 1.9.3.<sup>[58]</sup>

All calculated structures and imaginary frequencies were visualized with Chemcraft 1.8.<sup>[59]</sup>

### Catalyst molecular comparison

To assess the Lewis-acidity of the borane catalysts, we computed their fluoride ion affinity (FIA) at the ωB97X-D3/def2-TZVP level of theory in the gas phase under standard conditions (298.15 K, 1.00 atm). Additionally, we evaluated their hydride ion affinity (HIA) ⸺another established metric of Lewis acidity relevant for hydrogenation catalysts.<sup>[2]</sup> Both values were calculated as the negative reaction enthalpies of the following reactions:<sup>[60]</sup>

1) { \mathrm { F I A } } \colon { \mathrm { L A } } + { \mathrm { F } } ^ { - } \to [ { \mathrm { L A } } { \mathrm { - F } } ] ^ { - }

2) HIA: LA + H<sup>−</sup> → [LA-H]<sup>−</sup>

Table S4. FIA and HIA values of boranes
Catalyst | FIA, kJ/mol | %LAFIA | HIA, kJ/mol | %LAHIA
B1 | 467 | 100 | 519 | 100
B2 | 409 | 88 | 464 | 89
B3 | 423 | 91 | 477 | 92

Higher values indicate stronger Lewis acidity. The relative Lewis acidity (%LA) values are calculated by normalizing to catalyst B1 (set at 100%) using the formula: (Bx / B1) × 100. The similar trends observed for both FIA- and HIA-based acidity scales support the consistency and validity of these descriptors for evaluating Lewis acidity in this system.

The authors selected symmetrical 1,4-diphenylbutane-1,4-dione (1y) as their DFT model: equivalent carbonyl groups reduced the intermediates and conformers to consider. The original SI presents an energy diagram for reduction of the 2y-oxonium ion. That diagram is a private source record, not a figure supplied below or evidence of solver execution.

The zero level (0 kcal/mol) used as a reference for the estimation of relative stabilities corresponds to \mathrm { \bf B } 3 + \mathrm { \bf 1 } \mathrm { \bf y } + 2 \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } ; \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { \bf O } is included in all other energy points but is not depicted for simplicity.

The original SI labels Cartesian coordinates in angstrom, solution-phase G_sol at 353.15 K in Eh, and transition-state imaginary frequencies in cm^-1. ### Formation selectivity and product stability

The authors carried out DFT calculations on the diphenyl THF system 2y to investigate the origin of diastereoselectivity. Figure 1 belongs to the original article, not to the public input assets.

The transition state leading to the cis product ( \mathrm { T S } _ { c i s } ) was predicted to be 2.1 kcal/mol lower in energy than the one leading to the trans product ( \mathrm { T S } _ { t r a n s } ) which is in excellent agreement with experiments ( \Delta \Delta G ^ { \ddagger } = 2 . 1 kcal/mol; 20:1 dr, both calculated and observed). The barrier for reduction from the oxocarbenium intermediate Int-1y to \mathrm { T S } _ { c i s } is relatively low \left( \Delta G ^ { \ddagger } = 5 . 1 \mathrm { ~ k c a l / m o l } \right) , consistent with a facile process. The cis and trans products are nearly isoenergetic \left( \Delta \Delta G = 0 . 3 \mathrm { k c a l / m o l } \right) , indicating that stereoselectivity is kinetically controlled by the catalyst. ### Structural analyses and reported interpretation

The original SI presents density-gradient isosurfaces for cis/trans transition states of the Int-1y reduction model with B3 and B1. Its NCI colour code is blue for strongly attractive, green for weak van der Waals and red for strongly repulsive interactions. These source plots are not supplied public artifacts or evidence of a new analysis.

With catalyst B3, both the NCI analysis and interatomic distance analysis support a non-random C–H···aryl edge contact between the aliphatic cis-α-CH of the substrate and a \mathrm { C } s p ^ { 2 } carbon of the catalyst’s aromatic ring ( \mathrm { H } ^ { . . . } { \bf C } distance = 2.65 Å, ~0.25 Å shorter than the vdW sum). This interaction is observed in the \mathrm { T S } _ { c i s } but not in the \mathrm { T S } _ { t r a n s }

With catalyst B1, a similar interaction is detected (H···C distance = 2.76 Å, ~0.14 Å shorter than the vdW sum):

In addition, arene−perfluoroarene offset π−π stacking interactions are observed between Int-2y and B3 in both \mathrm { T S } _ { c i s } and \mathrm { T S } _ { t r a n s } The centroid separations (3.62 for \mathrm { T S } _ { c i s } and 3.61 Å for \mathrm { T S } _ { t r a n s } ) fall within the typical range for near-parallel aromatic stacking interactions (3.3–3.8 Å),<sup>[61]</sup> further supporting their presence.

Noncovalent interaction (NCI) analysis<sup>63</sup> revealed multiple weak van der Waals interactions between the catalyst and substrate 1y (key interactions are highlighted in Figure 1; full details are provided in the SI). Both \mathrm { T } \dot { \mathrm { S } } _ { c i s } and \mathrm { T S } _ { t r a n s } exhibit ofset arene−perfluoroarene π−π stacking (centroid separations { \sim } 3 . 6 \mathrm { \AA } ) , which may assist in orienting the oxocarbenium intermediate. However, because high selectivity was also observed for products lacking aromatic groups \left( \mathrm { e } . \mathrm { g } _ { \cdot } , \ 2 \mathrm { s } \right) , this interaction alone cannot account for stereocontrol. A more general and consistent feature is a weak C−H···aryl edge interaction between the α-hydrogen of the substrate and an aryl ring of the catalyst, present in \mathrm { T S } _ { c i s } ~ ( \mathrm { H } { \cdots } \mathrm { C s p } ^ { 2 } = 2 . 6 5 ~ \mathring { \mathrm { A } } ) but absent in \mathrm { T S } _ { t r a n s ^ { \ast } } \mathrm { A } similar interaction was identified for \mathrm { T S } _ { c i s } with catalyst B1 (see the SI), supporting its broader relevance.<sup>64,65</sup> These findings suggest that, in addition to steric efects, subtle noncovalent interactions may also play a role in stereocontrol.

The original SI presents density-gradient isosurfaces for cis/trans transition states of the Int-1y reduction model with B3 and B1. Its NCI colour code is blue for strongly attractive, green for weak van der Waals and red for strongly repulsive interactions. These source plots are not supplied public artifacts or evidence of a new analysis.

With catalyst B1, a similar interaction is detected (H···C distance = 2.76 Å, ~0.14 Å shorter than the vdW sum):

In addition, arene−perfluoroarene offset π−π stacking interactions are observed between Int-2y and B3 in both \mathrm { T S } _ { c i s } and \mathrm { T S } _ { t r a n s } The centroid separations (3.62 for \mathrm { T S } _ { c i s } and 3.61 Å for \mathrm { T S } _ { t r a n s } ) fall within the typical range for near-parallel aromatic stacking interactions (3.3–3.8 Å),<sup>[61]</sup> further supporting their presence.

Noncovalent interaction (NCI) analysis<sup>63</sup> revealed multiple weak van der Waals interactions between the catalyst and substrate 1y (key interactions are highlighted in Figure 1; full details are provided in the SI). Both \mathrm { T } \dot { \mathrm { S } } _ { c i s } and \mathrm { T S } _ { t r a n s } exhibit ofset arene−perfluoroarene π−π stacking (centroid separations { \sim } 3 . 6 \mathrm { \AA } ) , which may assist in orienting the oxocarbenium intermediate. However, because high selectivity was also observed for products lacking aromatic groups \left( \mathrm { e } . \mathrm { g } _ { \cdot } , \ 2 \mathrm { s } \right) , this interaction alone cannot account for stereocontrol. A more general and consistent feature is a weak C−H···aryl edge interaction between the α-hydrogen of the substrate and an aryl ring of the catalyst, present in \mathrm { T S } _ { c i s } ~ ( \mathrm { H } { \cdots } \mathrm { C s p } ^ { 2 } = 2 . 6 5 ~ \mathring { \mathrm { A } } ) but absent in \mathrm { T S } _ { t r a n s ^ { \ast } } \mathrm { A } similar interaction was identified for \mathrm { T S } _ { c i s } with catalyst B1 (see the SI), supporting its broader relevance.<sup>64,65</sup> These findings suggest that, in addition to steric efects, subtle noncovalent interactions may also play a role in stereocontrol.
